defaults.permitted_development: In Scotland, lowering a kerb to create a domestic access normally needs approval from the roads authority wherever it crosses a public footway. Planning permission is commonly only needed where the access is onto a classified road or where householder permitted development rights do not apply, but you should check both planning and roads requirements before any works start.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate planning height rule. Kerb levels, gradients and construction details are controlled through roads standards.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national depth allowance. The council will focus on whether a vehicle can enter, leave and stand within the site without overhanging the footway.
rules.boundary_rules: The crossing remains part of the public road. Roads consent is separate from planning permission and does not create any exclusive parking rights in front of the property.
rules.roof_rules: Dropped-kerb works have no roof element. The nearest equivalent design issue is how gradients, retaining edges and any related gateway or canopy are handled, because those parts may be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: The highway authority usually specifies the kerb and footway construction, so the main material choice sits in the private driveway behind it. Use durable, well-drained surfacing rather than finishes that shed water onto the pavement or fail under vehicle loading.

rules.permitted_development: In Scotland, lowering a kerb to create a domestic access normally needs approval from the roads authority wherever it crosses a public footway. In more urban authorities, planning permission is commonly also checked for accesses onto classified roads or where householder rights do not apply, so planning and roads should be considered together from the start.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate planning height rule. Kerb levels, gradients and construction details are controlled through roads standards.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national depth allowance. The site should have enough depth and manoeuvring space for a vehicle to clear the footway and avoid routine reversing conflicts.
rules.boundary_rules: The footway crossing stays part of the public road. Consent for it does not create a reserved space on the carriageway, and the authority may refuse a scheme because of street furniture, traffic regulation orders, visibility or pedestrian safety.
rules.roof_rules: Dropped-kerb works have no roof element. The nearest equivalent design issue is how gradients, retaining edges and any related gateway or canopy are handled, because those parts may be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: The highway authority usually specifies the kerb and footway construction, so the main material choice sits in the private driveway behind it. Use durable, well-drained surfacing rather than finishes that shed water onto the pavement or fail under vehicle loading.

restrictions.conservation_area: A dropped kerb that alters a historic frontage or boundary in a conservation area may require a closer planning check even where roads consent is also needed.
restrictions.listed_building: Forming or widening an access in the curtilage of a listed building can need listed building consent as well as any planning and roads approvals.

restrictions.listed_building: Forming or widening an access in the curtilage of a listed building can need listed building consent as well as any planning and roads approvals.

rules.permitted_development: In Scotland, lowering a kerb to create a domestic access normally needs approval from the roads authority wherever it crosses a public footway. In more urban authorities, planning permission is commonly also checked for accesses onto classified roads or where householder rights do not apply, so planning and roads should be considered together from the start.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate planning height rule. Kerb levels, gradients and construction details are controlled through roads standards.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national depth allowance. The site should have enough depth and manoeuvring space for a vehicle to clear the footway and avoid routine reversing conflicts.
rules.boundary_rules: The footway crossing stays part of the public road. Consent for it does not create a reserved space on the carriageway, and the authority may refuse a scheme because of street furniture, traffic regulation orders, visibility or pedestrian safety.
rules.roof_rules: Dropped-kerb works have no roof element. The nearest equivalent design issue is how gradients, retaining edges and any related gateway or canopy are handled, because those parts may be assessed separately.

rules.height_rules: There is no separate planning height allowance. Kerb construction follows road standards, while retaining edges and level changes are judged as associated works.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national depth limit, but the access should be proportionate and should not rely on an over-wide engineered opening in a sensitive roadside edge.
rules.boundary_rules: Changes to verges, ditches, stone walls and traditional entrance treatments can be more sensitive than the driveway use itself. Early checking with both roads and planning is sensible.
rules.roof_rules: Dropped-kerb works have no roof element. The nearest equivalent design issue is how gradients, retaining edges and any related gateway or canopy are handled, because those parts may be assessed separately.
rules.materials_rules: Keep the access design simple and ensure drainage is dealt with inside the site. Over-engineered aprons and highly urban materials can look out of place in protected landscapes.
